svg.aria-label: Diagram: comparing Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon MSK and Amazon Data Firehose on the axis that separates them, which is retention and replay rather than throughput. Kinesis Data Streams is a buffer that can be re-read, with a retention period running from a minimum of 24 hours to a maximum of 8,760 hours or 365 days, so a consumer found to be wrong can be fixed and the stream reprocessed from an earlier point. Its provisioned shards each support one megabyte per second or a thousand records per second of writes and two megabytes per second or two thousand records per second of reads, while on-demand streams begin at four megabytes per second of write throughput. Amazon MSK is open-source Apache Kafka, where AWS provides the control plane for creating, updating and deleting clusters while the customer uses Kafka data-plane operations and owns topic configuration including retention, with a minimum of one broker per Availability Zone. Amazon Data Firehose is a pipe rather than a buffer: it buffers incoming data only to a size or a time interval before delivering it, so there is no retention and nothing to re-read, and a transform applied in flight runs on the way to what becomes the only copy of the data. A panel records two Firehose defaults that surprise people: for Amazon S3 delivery it concatenates records without any delimiters unless newline delimiters are enabled, and it uses at-least-once semantics so retries may introduce duplicates for every destination type except Amazon S3, Apache Iceberg Tables and Snowflake.
svg.title: A buffer, a broker and a pipe — separated by what they keep
svg.text: All three carry the stream. Only two let you read it again.
The decision is normally made on throughput — the axis on which they differ least.
Whatever you configure — it is yours
You own the data plane: topics,
It buffers only to batch — to a size
or a time interval — then delivers.
A transform runs on the way to
Backfill — if the producer kept it.
Two Firehose defaults worth setting before the first query fails
• To S3 it “concatenates data without any delimiters” — a thousand JSON records in one object, no line breaks,
which most line-oriented tooling cannot read. Newline delimiters are a setting, and it is off.
• At-least-once delivery, so retries may duplicate — for every destination except S3, Iceberg Tables and Snowflake.
Operational surface, low to high: Firehose has none · Kinesis has a shard count and a consumer · MSK has the full Kafka model.
Each step up buys time: Firehose gives you now, Kinesis the last day to the last year, MSK whatever you configured.
Ask what happens on the day you find the consumer was wrong — not which one can carry the load. They all can.
